Connect the slope of a function to a step toward its minimum.
How can a local slope guide us toward a minimum? Start with a simple bowl-shaped function.
f of x equals x squared. Its derivative is two times x.
The derivative tells us which way the function rises. Gradient descent takes a small step in the opposite direction. The learning rate η sets the step size.
The next x equals the current x minus the learning rate times the derivative at the current x.
At x = 3, the derivative is 6. With η = 0.1, the next x is 2.4: a step left, toward zero. The slope gives the direction; the learning rate controls how far we move.
At x = 3, which direction reduces f(x) = x² for a small step?
Why this answer? Whatever comes to mind. (Optional)

Yes: a positive derivative means the function rises to the right. A small step left lowers f(x). Subtracting a positive gradient makes exactly that move. Try explaining why a very large step could still overshoot the minimum.

Look again at the sign: f′(3) = 6 is positive. Going right raises the function, while a small step left lowers it. Subtracting η · 6 from 3 moves left. Read the example, then try the prediction again.
Start with the slope: f′(3) = 6. A positive slope means the function rises as x increases. To lower it, take a small step in the other direction. Read the example, then try the prediction again.

The direction is left: f′(3) = 6, so subtracting a small positive multiple moves x toward zero. This preview ends the check after three attempts. A real teacher would use your reasoning to decide what to revisit; this authored mock does not assess it.
